--- title: "Hierarchical and model-based clustering" description: "One distance matrix, four linkage rules and four different answers; mixture models that give each station a probability instead of a label; and the index that measures how far two partitions disagree." order: 3 categories: [unsupervised] --- ## Two properties of k-means you may not want k-means has two properties you may not want. It insists on round clusters of comparable size, and it insists on $k$ before it will tell you anything. Two other families relax those, in different directions. **Hierarchical clustering** builds a whole tree of nested groupings in one pass, so you choose $k$ afterwards by deciding where to cut. **Mixture models** replace the hard label with a probability, so a station on a boundary is allowed to be 60% one thing and 40% another, which is a fairer description of most seabed. Both bring new decisions with them, and this page is mostly about one of those decisions, because it is the one that quietly determines the answer. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. The R tab is what produced the tables and figures you see; the Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent, shown for translation rather than executed by the site. Figures stay in R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. It is real code, not pseudocode: it runs against the same files through `python/mlbasic_data.py`, and `python/check-snippets.py` executes every snippet in the site to keep it honest. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly**: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## Hierarchical clustering The algorithm starts with every station as its own cluster and repeatedly merges the two closest, until everything is in one. Recording the order of merges gives a tree; cutting the tree at a height gives a partition. "The two closest" needs a definition, because after the first merge you are measuring the distance between *groups*, not points. That definition is the **linkage**: | Linkage | Distance between two groups is | | --- | --- | | **single** | the distance between their two closest members | | **complete** | the distance between their two furthest members | | **average** | the mean distance over all cross-group pairs | | **Ward** | the increase in within-cluster sum of squares caused by merging them | These sound like technical variants of one idea. They are not. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() community <- load_coastal_community() taxa_only <- community |> dplyr::select(starts_with("tax")) prepared <- recipe(~ ., data = taxa_only) |> step_log(all_numeric_predictors(), offset = 1) |> step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) |> prep() |> bake(new_data = NULL) |> as.matrix() distances <- dist(prepared) bottom <- community |> inner_join(dplyr::select(survey, station_id, substrate), by = "station_id") |> mutate(bottom = if_else(substrate %in% c("rock", "gravel"), "hard", "soft")) |> pull(bottom) linkages <- expand_grid(linkage = c("single", "average", "complete", "ward.D2"), k = 2:6) |> mutate(result = map2(linkage, k, \(method, k) { groups <- cutree(hclust(distances, method = method), k) tibble(agreement_with_substrate = adjustedRandIndex(groups, bottom), largest_cluster = max(table(groups)) / length(groups)) })) |> unnest(result) linkages |> dplyr::select(linkage, k, agreement_with_substrate) |> pivot_wider(names_from = k, values_from = agreement_with_substrate, names_prefix = "k=") |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|linkage | k=2| k=3| k=4| k=5| k=6| |:--------|-----:|-----:|-----:|-----:|-----:| |single | 0.005| 0.011| 0.021| 0.026| 0.032| |average | 0.026| 0.287| 0.284| 0.284| 0.279| |complete | 0.332| 0.843| 0.837| 0.381| 0.367| |ward.D2 | 0.889| 0.434| 0.402| 0.252| 0.249|
::: ::: ## Python ```python import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sklearn.cluster import AgglomerativeClustering from sklearn.metrics import adjusted_rand_score from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import FunctionTransformer, StandardScaler from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_community, load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() community = load_coastal_community() taxa_only = community.filter(like="tax") prepared = Pipeline([ ("log", FunctionTransformer(np.log1p, feature_names_out="one-to-one")), ("normalise", StandardScaler()), ]).fit_transform(taxa_only) bottom = np.where( community.merge(survey[["station_id", "substrate"]], on="station_id") ["substrate"].isin(["rock", "gravel"]), "hard", "soft") # scikit-learn's "ward" is R's ward.D2; the others carry the same names. linkages = pd.DataFrame([ {"linkage": method, "k": k, "agreement_with_substrate": adjusted_rand_score( AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=k, linkage=method) .fit_predict(prepared), bottom)} for method in ("single", "average", "complete", "ward") for k in range(2, 7) ]) (linkages.pivot(index="linkage", columns="k", values="agreement_with_substrate") .add_prefix("k=") .round(3) .reset_index()) ``` ::: Note that the tree is built once, from one distance matrix, and `cutree()` reads partitions off it for any $k$ you like. That is hierarchical clustering's real convenience. ## The adjusted Rand index The column we just filled needs defining, since it is how the rest of this section compares partitions to each other. Take every pair of stations. Two partitions **agree** about a pair if both put the pair together or both keep the pair apart. The proportion of pairs they agree about is the **Rand index**. Two random partitions already agree about most pairs, since with many clusters nearly every pair is "apart" in both, so the **adjusted** Rand index subtracts the agreement expected by chance and rescales: - **1**: identical partitions (cluster *labels* do not matter, only the grouping) - **0**: no more agreement than two random partitions of the same sizes - below 0: less agreement than chance `mclust::adjustedRandIndex()` computes it. Here we use it against the true hard/soft substrate split, which we know only because the data is simulated; in real work you would use it to compare two methods, or one method across two resamples. ## Reading the linkage comparison ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} linkage_panel <- function(column, label) { ggplot(linkages, aes(k, .data[[column]], colour = linkage)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point(size = 2.2) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2:6) + labs(x = "number of clusters (k)", y = label, colour = NULL) } (linkage_panel("agreement_with_substrate", "adjusted Rand index vs substrate") | linkage_panel("largest_cluster", "share of stations in largest cluster")) + plot_layout(guides = "collect") & theme(legend.position = "bottom") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The same 800 stations, the same distance matrix, four linkage rules. Left: agreement with the true hard/soft substrate split. Right: the share of stations swept into the single largest cluster.](beyond-k-means_files/figure-html/fig-linkage-1.png){#fig-linkage fig-alt='Two line charts against number of clusters from 2 to 6, one line per linkage rule. Left, adjusted Rand index against the true substrate split: Ward starts highest at 0.89 at k equals 2 then falls to about 0.25; complete linkage starts at 0.33, jumps to 0.84 at k equals 3, holds at k equals 4 then drops to about 0.37; average linkage stays between 0.03 and 0.29; single linkage never rises above 0.03. Right, share of stations in the largest cluster: single linkage stays above 0.99 throughout and average above 0.92, while complete falls from 0.92 to 0.47 and Ward from 0.78 to 0.28.' width=1800} ::: ::: **Single linkage fails completely.** At every $k$ from 2 to 6 it puts more than 99% of stations in one cluster and peels off one or two on their own. This is **chaining**: since the distance between groups is the distance between their nearest members, a thread of intermediate stations lets one group absorb another. On data with a continuous gradient running through it, there is always such a thread. Single linkage is an outlier detector here, not a clustering method. **Average linkage does the same thing more slowly**, still holding 92% of stations in one cluster at $k = 6$. **Complete and Ward both find the substrate split, at different $k$.** Ward gets it at $k = 2$ with an adjusted Rand index of **0.889**. Complete gets it at $k = 3$, scoring **0.843**, because it spends its first split isolating a group of 66 unusual stations, and only its second cut is the ecological one. So: one dataset, one distance matrix, five defensible values of $k$, and answers ranging from 0.005 to 0.889. The linkage is not a detail. ::: {.callout-warning} `hclust()`'s default linkage is `"complete"`. At the $k$ most people try first, $k = 2$, it scores 0.332 here, less than half of what Ward gets at the same $k$. Defaults are not recommendations. ::: Ward's advantage on this data is not an accident. Ward merges the pair that adds least to the within-cluster sum of squares, which is the quantity k-means minimises, so Ward and k-means are looking for the same kind of cluster, and they agree here almost exactly (adjusted Rand index 0.935 between their $k = 2$ partitions). If you want the tree *and* k-means-like behaviour, Ward is the linkage to ask for. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hier_fit <- workflow() |> add_recipe(recipe(~ ., data = taxa_only) |> step_log(all_numeric_predictors(), offset = 1) |> step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())) |> add_model(hier_clust(num_clusters = 2, linkage_method = "ward.D2")) |> fit(data = taxa_only) extract_cluster_assignment(hier_fit) |> count(.cluster) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|.cluster | n| |:---------|---:| |Cluster_1 | 179| |Cluster_2 | 621|
::: ::: ## Python ```python hier_fit = AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=2, linkage="ward").fit(prepared) (pd.Series(hier_fit.labels_ + 1) .value_counts() .sort_index() .reset_index(name="n") .rename(columns={"index": ".cluster"})) ``` ::: ## Mixture models: a probability instead of a label A **Gaussian mixture model** says the data was generated by a handful of overlapping multivariate normal distributions, and estimates their means, their shapes and how much of the data each one produced. Because it is a real probability model, it gives you two things k-means cannot: clusters that may be elongated or differently sized, and a posterior probability of membership for every station. `mclust` fits these, choosing both the number of components and the shape family by BIC. We fit it on the first five principal components rather than all 24 taxa, because a full covariance matrix in 24 dimensions has 300 free parameters per component. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} scores <- prcomp(prepared)$x[, 1:5] set.seed(104) mixture <- Mclust(scores, G = 1:6, verbose = FALSE) c(components = mixture$G, model = mixture$modelName, agreement_with_substrate = round(adjustedRandIndex(mixture$classification, bottom), 3)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> components model agreement_with_substrate #> "3" "VEV" "0.426" ``` ::: ::: ## Python ```python from sklearn.decomposition import PCA from sklearn.mixture import GaussianMixture scores = PCA(n_components=5).fit_transform(prepared) candidates = { (g, shape): GaussianMixture(n_components=g, covariance_type=shape, random_state=104, n_init=5).fit(scores) for g in range(1, 7) for shape in ("spherical", "diag", "tied", "full") } best = min(candidates, key=lambda key: candidates[key].bic(scores)) mixture = candidates[best] classification = mixture.predict(scores) + 1 pd.Series({ "components": best[0], "shape": best[1], "agreement_with_substrate": round( adjusted_rand_score(classification, bottom), 3), }) ``` ::: Three components, model `VEV`, meaning ellipsoids of equal volume with varying shape and orientation, and an adjusted Rand index against substrate of 0.426, far below Ward's 0.889. That is not a failure to find the substrate split; it is a decision to describe something else. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} community |> mutate(component = mixture$classification, bottom = bottom) |> inner_join(dplyr::select(survey, station_id, depth_m), by = "station_id") |> summarise(stations = n(), `hard bottom` = sum(bottom == "hard"), `median depth (m)` = round(median(depth_m), 1), .by = component) |> arrange(component) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| component| stations| hard bottom| median depth (m)| |---------:|--------:|-----------:|----------------:| | 1| 190| 184| 67.6| | 2| 337| 9| 122.6| | 3| 273| 1| 59.6|
::: ::: ## Python ```python (community.assign(component=classification, bottom=bottom) .merge(survey[["station_id", "depth_m"]], on="station_id") .groupby("component") .apply(lambda g: pd.Series({ "stations": len(g), "hard bottom": int((g["bottom"] == "hard").sum()), "median depth (m)": round(g["depth_m"].median(), 1), }), include_groups=False) .reset_index()) ``` ::: Component 1 is the hard bottom, essentially intact. Components 2 and 3 are the soft bottom cut in half along depth, at median depths of 123 m and 60 m. The mixture found the substrate boundary *and then* split a gradient, because a long curved cloud of stations is not one Gaussian, and BIC will buy a second Gaussian to cover it. This is the same result as the BIC choice on [the previous page](choosing-the-number-of-clusters.qmd), seen from the inside. The consolation is that the model tells you which stations it is unsure about. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tibble(PC1 = scores[, 1], PC2 = scores[, 2], component = factor(mixture$classification), uncertainty = mixture$uncertainty) |> ggplot(aes(PC1, PC2, colour = component, size = uncertainty)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.7) + scale_size_continuous(range = c(0.7, 4), breaks = c(0, 0.2, 0.4)) + labs(subtitle = "Point size is how unsure the model is of the assignment") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Mixture-model uncertainty, one point per station, on the first two principal components. Stations the model cannot confidently assign are not scattered at random: they line the boundary between the two soft-bottom components, which is a depth gradient with no real edge in it.](beyond-k-means_files/figure-html/fig-uncertainty-1.png){#fig-uncertainty fig-alt='Scatter plot of principal component 2 against principal component 1 for 800 stations, coloured by mixture component and sized by assignment uncertainty. Component 1 occupies the right-hand third of the plot, from PC1 about 1 to 6, as a loose cloud of its own whose points are nearly all small. Components 2 and 3 together fill the left and lower centre as one continuous cloud, component 2 above and component 3 below, with no gap between them. The large points marking uncertain assignments run in a diagonal band through the middle of that cloud where the two colours meet, and are almost absent from its outer edges and from component 1.' width=1300} ::: ::: The median station has an uncertainty of 0.002, so the model is sure about almost everything. But **69 stations have an uncertainty above 0.25**, and they are not spread evenly: they sit where components 2 and 3 meet, which is the middle of the depth gradient. That is the honest answer for a station halfway along a continuum, and a hard partition simply never reports it. ## Limits of trees and mixtures **A dendrogram looks more authoritative than it is.** It is a picture of one linkage's merge order. Change the linkage and you get a different tree from the same data, as the table above shows, and nothing in the picture warns you. **Hierarchical clustering is greedy and final.** A merge made early is never undone, so an early mistake propagates all the way up the tree. **It costs memory.** The distance matrix is $n(n-1)/2$ entries: fine for 800 stations, about 12 GB for 50,000 CTD profiles. **Mixture models assume Gaussian components.** Community counts are not Gaussian even after a log transform, which is part of why we ran the mixture on principal-component scores. The components you get back are features of the fitted density, not species assemblages, and the two coincide only sometimes. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Key points - Hierarchical clustering builds one tree and lets you cut it at any $k$ afterwards. - **The linkage rule decides the answer.** On the same distance matrix, agreement with the true split ranged from 0.005 (single) to 0.889 (Ward). - Single and average linkage **chain**: they peel off one station at a time and leave 99% of the data in a single cluster. Suspect chaining whenever one cluster holds almost everything. - `hclust()` defaults to complete linkage, which scored 0.332 at $k = 2$ here. Ward is the sensible default when you want k-means-like clusters with a tree attached. - The **adjusted Rand index** compares two partitions pair by pair: 1 is identical, 0 is chance. - Mixture models return a probability per station. Here 69 stations were genuinely ambiguous, all of them on the depth gradient, which is information a hard partition throws away. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Cut the Ward tree at $k = 2$ and the complete-linkage tree at $k = 3$ and compare them with `adjustedRandIndex()`. They score 0.889 and 0.843 against substrate: how similar are they to *each other*? 2. Run `Mclust()` on the first two principal components instead of five. Does it still choose three components, and does the uncertainty band survive?
